text: An executive framework for deciding what AI can do without human approval An AI agent flags a transaction as likely fraud. It can retrieve account history, compare patterns, open a case, send a customer message, freeze a card, and issue a refund. The engineering team may be able to connect every step. Leadership still has to decide which actions the agent should perform without a human. That decision changes architecture, access design, testing, operations, and accountability. text: Video title: How Much Autonomy Should You Give an AI Agent? | AI Governance. Description: 🤖 How much autonomy should an AI agent have? This short video introduces the AI Agent Authority Framework, a practical way for technology and business leaders to decide what an AI agent should be allowed to do without human approval. The framework separates delegated authority into five levels: 👁️ Level 1: Observe 💡 Level 2: Recommend ✋ Level 3: Act with approval 🛡️ Level 4: Act within defined boundaries ⚙️ Level 5: Execute an autonomous workflow Level 5 is not always the goal. The appropriate level depends on the impact of a mistake, whether the action can be reversed, what systems and data the agent can access, the strength of monitoring and recovery controls, and who remains accountable for the outcome.
